item.title: SensEnhance: A Genetic Circuit for Converting Endogenous Mammalian Gene Signals Into High-Dynamic-Range Genetic Readouts.
item.abstract: Integrating synthetic gene circuits with endogenous mammalian gene expression programs enables genetic readouts of physiologically relevant cellular states. However, the performance of these readouts is often constrained by sensing promoters with low maximal output, modest fold changes, and high basal activity. Here, we use mathematical modeling and analysis to devise SensEnhance, a generalizable genetic circuit architecture that converts leaky, low-dynamic-range promoter signals into tightly controlled, high-dynamic-range outputs. SensEnhance combines sequestration-mediated suppression below a tunable response threshold with feedback-supported amplification above it. We implement SensEnhance through split intein-mediated protein trans-splicing and experimentally validate its predicted input-output behavior and threshold tunability. We apply SensEnhance to a YAP/TAZ-responsive mechanosensing promoter and stably integrate the circuit into NIH/3T3 fibroblasts, increasing output fold change between soft and stiff tissue-like hydrogels from 2.6-fold in the promoter-only configuration to over 20-fold using SensEnhance. When coupled to a STAT3-responsive promoter showing a 2.5-fold change in response to IL-6, SensEnhance increases this fold change to 14-fold, improving cytokine sensing and supporting its generic applicability across signaling pathways. These results establish SensEnhance as a modular strategy for improving the dynamic range and tunability of mammalian genetic biosensors.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Synthetic Biology Promises and Challenges.
item.abstract: The development of biological systems often requires extensive experimental iterations and optimization, which can be resource-intensive and time-consuming. In recent years, rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have demonstrated a strong potential to address these challenges. AI technologies, particularly those that enable continuous learning from large datasets and intelligent exploration of novel solution spaces, align closely with the evolving needs of synthetic biology platforms. AI holds significant promise for analyzing complex biological features and facilitating the design of sophisticated biological systems. This review explores the current progress of AI applications in synthetic biology, focusing on its impact in areas such as part engineering, circuit engineering, metabolic engineering, and genome engineering. It also highlights several key challenges in integrating AI with synthetic biology, including issues related to standardized data, development of intelligent platforms, automation of experimentation, and enhancing predictive accuracy. The fusion of AI and synthetic biology is poised to revolutionize the "design-build-test-learn" (DBTL) cycle by accelerating the design and testing of new biological systems. Furthermore, the development of AI systems that emulate the capabilities of synthetic biologists could lead to significant breakthroughs in AI itself. As both fields continue to evolve in tandem, the convergence of AI and synthetic biology holds the potential to drive innovations that will reshape the future of biotechnology and artificial intelligence.

item.title: NanoBlocks: Creating Genetically Encoded Protein Switches Using Competitive Binding.
item.abstract: Many regulatory mechanisms function by changing a molecule's conformation such that it is switched between active and inactive states. Engineering macromolecules such as proteins to show robust conformational changes in response to arbitrary, well-defined molecular stimuli is of great interest in fields such as synthetic biology and nanoscale engineering, because it allows the development of "smart" molecular tools. We present a strategy that can convert "simple" affinity binders such as nanobodies into protein switches that undergo clear structural rearrangements in response to their innate targets, by introducing a peptide that competes for the binding site. We demonstrate proof-of-concept implementations of this "NanoBlock" design by developing genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors based on two entirely different binder frameworks, the ALFA nanobody and the PDZ domain of Erbin. We show that our design allows the construction of well-performing protein switches that can reliably detect their targets in vitro, in mammalian cells, as part of fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) experiments, and that also generalizes to the creation of stimulus-responsive enzymes via the integration of a bioluminescent readout. We furthermore develop a theoretical model that rationalizes the observations and provides insight into the underlying molecular mechanisms. Overall, our strategy expands the possibilities to create "smart" protein-based molecules and effectors.

item.title: High-throughput identification of chromatin-opening transcription factors
item.abstract: Cell fate transitions involve major changes to the chromatin landscape, some of which are thought to deepen the basin around a newly adopted cell state, stabilizing gene expression programs that might otherwise be transient. Transcription factors (TFs) are central to this process, binding only a subset of the genome-wide occurrences of their cognate motifs to create accessible regions that can act as cell type-specific enhancers. However, apart from a few well-studied cases, it is not clear which of the ~1,600 mammalian TFs can directly or indirectly initiate newly accessible sites, nor why only some motif occurrences gain accessibility. Here, we performed pooled CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) screens to upregulate endogenous developmental TFs in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) and assess their impact on the chromatin landscape. Following a pre-screen of 240 developmental TFs for their capacity to elicit strong changes to the transcriptome, we prioritized 60 TFs for a well-powered CRISPRa multiome screen in which we jointly profiled gene expression and chromatin accessibility across ~140,000 single cells. We identify TFs that appear to initiate new chromatin accessibility on their own ("autonomous"), others whose chromatin-opening activity appears dependent on coincident binding of co-TFs heterogeneously expressed across mESCs ("opportunistic"), and yet others which appear to induce a co-TF and then act alongside it ("hierarchical"). Taken together, our findings suggest that the ability of a TF to "pioneer" chromatin opening, when it is newly expressed at physiological levels, strongly depends on the cell state and gene regulatory network it lands in. Looking forward, a comprehensive charting of such dependencies will inform how cell fate transitions are initiated in development, homeostasis and disease, and how to engineer them in silico, in vitro and in vivo.

item.title: pH-Responsive Synthetic Cells for Programmable In Situ Protein Synthesis and Release.
item.abstract: Lipid membrane-bound synthetic cells provide programmable, cell-like compartments for on-demand biomolecule production. However, most cell-free gene expression systems in synthetic cells are regulated by user-imposed cues rather than signals associated with environmental or physiological states. Here, we present an acidity-transducing synthetic cell that converts external pH changes into nucleic acid information to drive in situ protein synthesis. The system integrates gramicidin A proton channels for pH sensing, triplex-forming single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) that releases a trigger ssDNA upon acidification, and a toehold switch RNA that activates translation in response to the released trigger ssDNA. This work further reveals that tuning the annealing length between the pH-responsive and trigger ssDNAs controls the trigger-release pH, which is critical for enabling acid-triggered protein synthesis. The synthetic cells retain their pH-responsive activity when embedded in alginate hydrogels, creating acidity-responsive materials that synthesize proteins in situ rather than release preloaded cargo. Cell-penetrating peptide tagging further enables selective protein release and target-specific binding. This work establishes a molecular transduction strategy for programming synthetic cell materials to sense environmentally relevant acidity and generates functional biomolecules on demand.

item.title: Synthetic Biology-Based Biomanufacturing: Current Status and Future Prospects.
item.abstract: Biomanufacturing, which utilizes biological systems to produce chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and materials, has undergone transformative changes in recent decades, evolving from traditional genetic engineering-based production systems to new platforms based on synthetic biology. This chapter provides an in-depth overview of the development of biomanufacturing under the influence of synthetic biology and discusses various tools and strategies of artificial intelligence for pathway design, construction, and optimization, which play a crucial role in overcoming the limitations of traditional methods. However, data barriers, insufficient model interpretability, and generalizability challenges remain the current major bottlenecks. In the future, with interdisciplinary integration and technological iteration, synthetic biology will drive the evolution of biomanufacturing towards a sustainable bioeconomy, ultimately forming a new paradigm of green and low-carbon industrial production.

item.title: Multiplexed single-molecule analysis of barcoded protein variants.
item.abstract: Single-molecule techniques provide exceptional resolution of biomolecular dynamics but are limited by low throughput. Here, we present a DNA barcoding strategy that enables parallel kinetic profiling of multiple protein variants in a single experiment. Each protein is covalently linked to a unique DNA barcode, decoded through transient hybridisation of fluorescent probes distinguished by colour and binding duration. Applied to a library of 16 ClpS variants, this approach revealed ~5-fold variation in dissociation kinetics and uncovered previously unrecognised bimodal binding behaviour arising from distinct structural subpopulations. By enabling scalable, multiplexed functional characterisation at the single-molecule level, this platform provides a general framework for protein engineering, directed evolution and the development of next-generation single-molecule technologies.

item.title: Cell-free expression and NGS-powered substrate profiling reveal a thermostable metagenomic meganuclease from an extreme environment with novel specificity.
item.abstract: As an alternative to historical enzyme isolation, metagenomic databases (e.g. MGnify) provide information on vast unculturable microbial diversity, including extreme environments, and constitute an enormous source of functional proteins. Conservative mining of these data by close sequence homology alone tends to identify merely different versions of known enzymes. Here we present a discovery strategy for meganucleases based on wider capture of less homologous enzymes in metagenomic databases, and incorporating metadata with their homology. We use cell-free expression to bypass host incompatibility and the need for purification, along with deep sequencing for experimental assessment of substrate specificity and cleavage pattern, thereby circumventing classical gel-based profiling. Specifically, we discovered the temperature-stable (>55°C), intron-encoded LAGLIDADG meganuclease I-MG11 that recognizes a GC-rich 17 base pair sequence to generate 4-nt palindromic 3'-overhangs-the first monomeric meganuclease to produce such overhangs. Co-folding models of I-MG11 bound to DNA provide a structural context for enzyme-DNA interactions, highlighting differences from other monomeric LAGLIDADG meganucleases (e.g. I-SceI) shaped by InDels (insertion-deletions) in the DNA-binding region that may cause specificity changes. Our strategy streamlines general bona fide identification and annotation of meganucleases, while the unique properties of I-MG11 expand the toolbox of molecular genome engineering.

item.title: Enzyme systems immobilized using metal-organic frameworks as plant cell mimics for converting CO2 into organic matter: Feasibility, design principles and translational challenges.
item.abstract: Plant cells convert carbon dioxide into organic matter by coupling carbon acquisition, energy conversion, enzymatic fixation and product synthesis within spatially organized compartments. Reconstructing these functions outside living cells could provide a programmable route to low-carbon synthesis, but dispersed enzymes lack the stability and transport control of chloroplasts. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) offer a tunable scaffold for enriching CO2, immobilizing enzymes and organizing cofactor regeneration and reaction sequences. This review evaluates whether these functions can be integrated into plant-cell-mimetic systems that produce C1 compounds (formate and methanol), C2-C4 metabolic intermediates, sugars, storage polymers and biomass-like mixtures. We connect evidence from enzyme-MOF biocomposites, artificial chloroplasts, synthetic carbon-fixation cycles, photoenzymatic CO2 reduction, artificial CO2-concentrating mechanisms and continuous-flow biocatalysis to identify requirements that change with pathway and product complexity. Integrated proof-of-concept systems already support MOF-enabled CO2-to-C1 conversion. More complex synthesis remains limited by cofactor economy, oxygen and reactive‑oxygen-species damage, enzyme stoichiometry, framework stability and product transport. For ATP-dependent routes, sustained ATP regeneration must also be matched to NAD(P)H supply and carbon flux. We propose modular architectures, quantitative evaluation criteria and a staged development roadmap. Hierarchically compartmentalized or serial-flow platforms appear most practical because they allow carbon capture, energy conversion, fixation and product-forming modules to operate under compatible conditions and to be replaced independently. Their environmental value must ultimately be established through full-system energy and life-cycle carbon balances.

item.title: Synthetic biology for sustainable abundance: biomining, electromicrobial production, and hyper-engineerable microbes.
item.abstract: Over the next few decades, there is a compelling need to build a new sustainable energy infrastructure to replace the fossil fuel system that we have relied on since the 1700s. This infrastructure must not only replace what exists but also far exceed its capabilities, delivering more power to more people to meet the growing demands from both developing and advanced economies. But how do we increase energy use without harming the Earth? Biology drives the Earth's geochemical cycles, operating with far greater elemental and energy fluxes than all of human civilization. This suggests that synthetic biology could solve at least some of our environmental problems while providing access to much greater energy. However, leveraging biology remains a formidable challenge, in part because we do not yet understand nearly enough about the basic science underlying the biological systems that bring the most unusual and useful capabilities to sustainability and energy. This challenge is not unique to biology and sustainability - groundbreaking technologies of the past have required not only curiosity-driven basic research but also use-inspired basic research. Over the past decade, our lab has discovered new basic science needed to build synthetic biology technologies and established itself as a leader in sustainability and synthetic biology. This review summarizes breakthroughs from our lab over the past decade in three key areas: biomining, electrically driven metabolism, and hyper-engineerable microbes.

item.title: De novo design of miniprotein inhibitors of bacterial adhesins.
item.abstract: The rise of multidrug-resistant bacterial infections necessitates the discovery of novel antimicrobial strategies. Here, we show that protein design provides a generalizable means of generating new antimicrobials by neutralizing the function of bacterial adhesins, which are virulence factors critical in host-pathogen interactions. We de novo designed high-affinity miniprotein binders to FimH and Abp chaperone usher pili adhesins from uropathogenic Escherichia coli and Acinetobacter baumannii, respectively, which are implicated in mediating both uncomplicated and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTI) responsible for significant morbidity worldwide. The designed antagonists have high specificity and stability, disrupt bacterial recognition of host receptors, block biofilm formation, and are effective in treating and preventing murine models of uncomplicated and catheter-associated UTIs in vivo.

item.title: Bioinspired dynamic self-assembling condensates driven by liquid-liquid phase separation for therapeutic system innovation and applications: A review.
item.abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), a key biophysical phenomenon in cellular physiology and pathology, profoundly influences cellular homeostasis and disease progression. Notably, the development of biomimetic intervention strategies based on LLPS principles has emerged as a frontier in disease therapy. This review systematically elucidated the molecular basis and regulatory networks of LLPS, with particular emphasis on its emerging applications in therapeutic development: (1) precise interventions targeting the dynamic properties of pathogenic condensates, offering breakthrough tools for tackling refractory diseases; (2) construction of next-generation responsive delivery platforms by harnessing phase transition and dynamic assembly properties, enabling spatiotemporally precise treatment; and (3) LLPS-powered intelligent biomimetic artificial cells, expanding the boundaries of synthetic biology. We further provided an in-depth analysis of urgent challenges, including decoding of LLPS core mechanisms, the difficulty in selectively distinguishing pathological from physiological condensates, the bottleneck of precise controllability in delivery systems, limited in vivo stability and immunogenicity data of LLPS-based delivery systems, and challenges in engineering controllability and large-scale production. Finally, we outlined potential future research directions, suggesting that integrating LLPS studies with multidisciplinary approaches could provide new strategies and technical support to address these challenges.

item.title: The synthetic biology frontier: engineered oncolytic viruses and viral vectors for next-generation cancer therapy and gene delivery.
item.abstract: Viruses are no longer used merely as naturally occurring tools for gene transfer or as blunt cytolytic agents. Researchers are rewriting their genomes, capsids, tropisms, regulatory elements, and payloads to create therapeutic systems that sense disease, execute conditional programs, and remodel pathological tissue. In oncology, engineered oncolytic viruses (OVs) can combine tumor-selective replication with immunogenic cell death, antigen release, and local immune stimulation. In parallel, viral-vector engineering, particularly AAV and LVs, is addressing central limitations of gene delivery: the prevalence of pre-existing neutralizing antibodies, the difficulty of systemic administration and repeat dosing (AAV), and the manufacturing bottleneck of ex vivo cell therapies (LV). The clinical record is encouraging but uneven: T-VEC has shown that an engineered herpes simplex virus can improve durable responses in selected melanoma lesions, while G47Δ/teserpaturev and newer armed HSV platforms provide evidence of feasibility, safety, and occasional durable responses in difficult solid tumors. Lentiviral vector-based in vivo CAR-T cell generation, exemplified by KLN-1010/inMMyCAR and related first-in-human programs, signals a paradigm shift away from ex vivo manufacturing. However, the broader field has not converted its large preclinical literature into a proportional number of clinically meaningful, systemically deployable medicines. The main bottlenecks remain delivery, tumor heterogeneity, immune clearance, suboptimal pharmacodynamic biomarkers, manufacturing complexity, resistance, and the difficulty of proving benefit for products with delayed or immunologically mediated effects. This review examines the synthetic biology toolkit for programmable viral therapeutics through a unified engineering framework that integrates OVs, AAV, and LVs by design principle rather than by vector class. We discuss tumor-selective promoters, microRNA detargeting, retargeted capsids and ligands, attenuation, genome-scale assembly, immune-stimulatory payloads, bispecific and trispecific engagers, logic-gated circuits, safety switches, serodivergent AAV capsids, biomimetic cloaking, cell carriers, biomaterial delivery systems, and in vivo CAR-T generation. Our central thesis is that the next generation of viral medicines will be selected not by the most elaborate genome, but by the most coherent alignment of five measurable success factors: tumor selectivity, immune remodeling, delivery and biodistribution, controllable safety, and manufacturability. The emerging paradigm is therefore programmable viral therapeutics: context-sensitive biological medicines designed to operate within the constraints of human tumors and human immunity.

item.title: Genome Editing of Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurological Disease: Progress and Translational Barriers.
item.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared mechanism across neurological disease. Specifically, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial DNA damage are factors in primary mitochondrial disorders and major neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson, Alzheimer, and Huntington diseases, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This review surveys the mechanisms driving mitochondrial dysfunction and evaluates the current landscape of gene-editing technologies developed to address them. We examine mitochondria-targeted editors and nuclear-targeted editors, examining the editing capability, delivery constraints, and off-target risk of each. Heteroplasmy-shifting nucleases currently offer the strongest in vivo evidence for mtDNA-directed therapy, while base editors extend correction to homoplasmic mutations at the cost of a narrower editing scope and off-target editing. Nuclear editing platforms avoid the mitochondrial gRNA import barrier entirely, allowing current technologies to achieve the most progress toward functional, behavioral rescue in animal models. Across all platforms, delivery efficiency, off-target specificity, and translation from rodent to primate models remain unresolved barriers to clinical application. Gene editing for mitochondrial dysfunction is highly creditable as a precision therapy for genetically defined disease subsets, including primary mitochondrial disease and other neurodegenerative disorders with a known nuclear driver, rather than as a universal strategy for sporadic neurodegeneration, where mitochondrial dysfunction arises from multifactorial and poorly localized causes.

item.title: Identification of Kinome Biomarkers and Therapeutic Rescue in cGMP-Linked Retinal Degeneration
item.abstract: Inherited retinal degenerations, such as Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) and Leber's congenital amaurosis (LCA), are major causes of progressive and irreversible vision loss. The large number of genes associated with these disorders makes their clinical and molecular characterization difficult, while systemic biomarkers for disease progression or treatment response remain limited. These challenges were addressed by targeting cGMP-associated mechanisms shared by RP and LCA and integrating systemic biomarker profiling with retinal outcomes. Kinase activity analysis (kinome analysis) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells distinguished healthy and diseased states and captured therapy-associated signatures in rd10 mice treated with LP-CN03, a liposomal formulation of the cGMP analog CN03. This first systemic analysis in a therapeutically responsive animal model highlights kinome analysis as a potential translational readout. Given shared cGMP signaling in RP and AIPL1-associated LCA, LP-CN03's therapeutic potential was further evaluated in a new CRISPR-Cas9-generated Aipl1-/- mouse model. Treatment with LP-CN03 preserved retinal structure and function, as shown by electroretinography, longitudinal optical coherence tomography, fundus imaging, optomotor testing, and photoreceptor-specific gene expression. Together, these findings provide independent in vivo evidence for the neuroprotective effect of LP-CN03 in both cGMP-related RP and LCA, also highlighting the translational value of kinome profiling.
